\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\title{Community Health Access Survey: 2026 Field Report}
\author{Survey Unit, Regional Health Observatory}
\date{June 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We surveyed 466 households across urban, suburban, and rural tracts.
The questionnaire covered visit frequency, travel time, insurance status, and satisfaction.
Median annual visits decline steadily from urban to rural tracts.
Satisfaction follows the same gradient and drops sharply past thirty minutes of travel.
Targeted transport support emerges as the most promising policy lever.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
Access to primary care remains uneven across the region.
Rural residents travel farther for routine visits and report longer waits for appointments.
Urban clinics are closer on average but struggle with crowded schedules.
The 2026 field survey was designed to measure these gaps with a consistent instrument.
It is the third wave of a panel that began in 2022.
Earlier waves documented rising costs and shrinking clinic hours.
This wave shifts the focus to travel burden and patient satisfaction.
Field staff described the response rate as "remarkably strong" in their weekly briefings.
We surveyed 466 households across urban, suburban, and rural tracts.
The questionnaire covered visit frequency, travel time, insurance status, and satisfaction.
Local clinics helped distribute invitations and hosted interview sessions.
Community centers provided space for interviews in every stratum.
The survey period ran from February through April.
Interviewers worked in pairs and logged responses on tablet devices.
All respondents gave informed consent before the interview began.
Participation was voluntary and uncompensated.
The regional health authority reviewed the protocol in advance.
Findings from this wave will inform the 2027 transport subsidy pilot.
The steering group met monthly to review field progress.
Preliminary briefs went to participating clinics in May.
\section{Background}
Household surveys remain the workhorse of access research.
Administrative records miss households that never reach a clinic.
Travel burden has been measured in many ways across the literature.
Some studies use straight-line distance to the nearest facility.
Others rely on self-reported travel time, as this survey does.
Self-reports track perceived burden better than map distance.
The 2022 wave of this panel used a shorter instrument.
It found suggestive gaps between urban and rural respondents.
The 2024 wave added the travel module used again here.
Question wording stayed fixed across the two most recent waves.
That consistency supports the trend analysis in this report.
Funding for the 2026 wave came from the regional health authority.
\section{Methods}
We used a stratified sampling frame based on census tracts.
Each tract was assigned to the urban, suburban, or rural stratum.
Households were drawn at random within each stratum.
One adult per household was eligible to complete the interview.
Interviewers made up to three contact attempts before substitution.
Substitution stayed within the same stratum and block group.
The questionnaire was piloted with 24 households in January.
Pilot feedback shortened the travel module by four items.
The field protocol followed five steps.
\begin{itemize}
\item Recruit participants through community centers and clinics.
\item Administer the baseline questionnaire in a face-to-face interview.
\item Conduct a monthly follow-up call for three consecutive months.
\item Code responses and enter them into the regional registry.
\item Audit a ten percent subsample of completed interviews.
\end{itemize}
Staff called the coding stage "the bottleneck" because of handwritten notes.
Interviews lasted about forty minutes on average.
Follow-up calls lasted about ten minutes each.
Respondents could skip any question without giving a reason.
Skipped items were coded as missing rather than imputed.
The registry assigns each household a pseudonymous identifier.
Only the survey unit can re-identify records, under a signed data agreement.
Audio recordings were kept for the audited subsample only.
The audit compared registry entries against the recordings line by line.
\section{Results}
Response rates exceeded the pre-registered target in every stratum.
Urban tracts returned 212 completed interviews.
Suburban tracts returned 158, and rural tracts returned 96.
The completion rate among contacted households was 61 percent overall.
All estimates use the post-stratification weights described above.
Weighted and unweighted estimates differ by less than two points.
Item nonresponse stayed below four percent for every module.
The table below summarizes the key indicators by stratum.
\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\hline
Stratum & Respondents & Median visits & Satisfaction (\%) \\
\hline
Urban & 212 & 4.1 & 78 \\
Suburban & 158 & 3.6 & 71 \\
Rural & 96 & 2.8 & 64 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Median annual visits decline steadily from urban to rural tracts.
Satisfaction follows the same gradient.
Travel time accounts for much of the difference in a regression check.
Respondents in rural tracts reported a median one-way trip of 42 minutes.
Urban respondents reported a median trip of 11 minutes.
Several interviewees called the shuttle pilot "a lifeline" for elderly patients.
The figure below plots satisfaction against median travel time.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\fbox{\rule{0pt}{4cm}\rule{6cm}{0pt}}
\end{figure}
Satisfaction drops sharply once one-way travel exceeds thirty minutes.
The gradient is steepest among respondents over age sixty-five.
Insurance status does not explain the gradient on its own.
\section{Discussion}
The results point to distance as the central barrier in this region.
Subsidized transport may matter more than additional clinic capacity.
Building new clinics takes years; a shuttle network can start in months.
The shuttle pilot drew praise that one coordinator called "well deserved".
We caution that the survey window excluded the winter storm season.
Storm-related closures could widen the measured gaps.
Distance also interacts with clinic hours in rural tracts.
Clinics there close earlier on weekdays.
Evening appointments were rare outside urban tracts.
The 2022 wave hinted at the same gradient with a smaller sample.
This wave confirms it with a pre-registered design.
The sample underrepresents migrant workers who move between tracts.
Their access patterns likely differ from settled households.
Night-shift workers are also underrepresented.
Interviews were scheduled mostly during daytime hours.
Future waves should oversample mobile populations.
Future waves should also offer evening interview slots.
The registry will support a targeted follow-up study in 2027.
That study will track the same households through the winter season.
\section{Limitations}
Several limitations qualify these findings.
The sample frame excludes households without a registered address.
Informal settlements are therefore underrepresented.
Interviews were conducted only in the two official languages.
Respondents who prefer other languages may answer differently.
Recall error may affect reported visit counts.
Travel times are self-reported and may be rounded upward.
The satisfaction scale has not been validated in rural tracts.
Follow-up attrition reached 18 percent by the third call.
Attrition was higher among younger respondents.
Weighting corrects only part of this imbalance.
Results should not be extrapolated beyond the study region.
\section{Data Availability}
The anonymized registry extract is available on request.
Request forms are reviewed by the data agreement board.
Codebooks accompany every extract.
Interview recordings are destroyed after the audit window.
Replication materials accompany this report.
\section{Conclusion}
The 2026 wave documents a clear urban-rural gradient in access.
The gradient tracks travel time more than insurance status.
Targeted transport support emerges as the most promising lever.
The 2027 wave will test that lever directly.
The survey unit will publish the anonymized registry extract.
Field costs stayed within the approved budget.
The steering group approved public release in June.
\end{document}
